weeks.title: First conversations
weeks.summary: Start with a line of output, then let the person at the keyboard join in.

weeks.title: Words into stories
weeks.summary: Collect information, shape strings, and turn a handful of answers into something personal.

weeks.title: Making numbers useful
weeks.summary: Convert text to numbers and use arithmetic to answer everyday questions.

weeks.title: A little more precision
weeks.summary: Put formulas, decimal formatting, and an optional tip to work.

weeks.title: Choose your own path
weeks.summary: Make programs respond differently to different answers, from grades to an adventure.

weeks.title: Decisions with depth
weeks.summary: Combine rules, track state, and build a story where earlier choices matter.

weeks.title: Keep going, keep guessing
weeks.summary: Use loops to ask again, give feedback, and keep a game running until the goal is reached.

weeks.title: Loops with a little adventure
weeks.summary: Use for loops, enumerate, and repeated input to inspect letters and build a colorful word quest.

projects.title: Hello, world
projects.summary: The first building block: send a greeting to the screen.
steps: A quoted string holds the words that will appear.
print() sends that string to the console.
projects.explanation: This one statement is a complete program. Everything between the quotation marks is text.
projects.note: There is no input in this program; each run prints the same greeting.

projects.title: Favorite color conversation
projects.summary: Ask permission to start a conversation, then respond to someone's favorite color.
steps: Store the answer to a yes-or-no question.
The two if statements check for the exact words yes and no.
The chosen color is inserted into a friendly response.
projects.explanation: An if statement makes the next indented lines conditional on the answer.
projects.note: The first answer is case-sensitive in the original: type yes or no in lowercase. The color itself is converted to lowercase.

projects.title: Variables & first inputs
projects.summary: Watch a variable change from a whole number to a decimal to a name.
steps: The same variable holds 5, then 10.0, then bill.
input() returns text, which the program prints back.
int() changes a numeric answer into a whole number.
projects.explanation: input() always produces text; int() converts that text into a number.
projects.note: These are class notes and experiments. The favorite number is stored but never printed.

projects.title: A name with an introduction
projects.summary: Format a first and last name into a familiar, dramatic introduction.
steps: Keep the first and last name in separate variables.
capitalize() uppercases the first letter and lowercases the rest.
An f-string places those values inside a sentence.
projects.explanation: The expression inside braces is evaluated before the finished sentence is printed.
projects.note: capitalize() is simple formatting; names such as McDonald will become Mcdonald.

projects.title: Make a ridiculous story
projects.summary: Supply nine words and see them become an unexpected little adventure.
steps: Ask for an adjective, an animal, three verbs, and a few story details.
Each f-string inserts an answer into a fixed story template.
Separator lines and blank lines make the output easier to read.
projects.explanation: The variables are placeholders. Changing the answers changes the story without changing its structure.
projects.note: The browser version uses the same story template. Sample words are fictional.

projects.title: Build an ID badge
projects.summary: Turn contact details and favorite things into a neatly formatted ID card.
steps: Read a name, contact information, a title, an ID, and four favorites.
Slices take the first three, next three, and remaining digits.
A width of 30 places favorites in two columns.
projects.explanation: A slice selects a portion of a string without changing the original characters.
projects.note: Use ten phone digits without punctuation to match the original slicing. The sample badge uses fictional details.

projects.title: The big-number multiplier
projects.summary: Convert a number from text and multiply it by 293,884,955.
steps: The answer starts as a string.
The result is the input times a fixed constant.
projects.explanation: Conversion makes multiplication arithmetic instead of string repetition.
projects.note: The unusually large multiplier is exactly the constant in the original practice file.

projects.title: Text or a number?
projects.summary: See why repeating the string 7 is different from multiplying the number 7.
steps: The dog's name and favorite number both arrive as text.
Multiplying the original string by three repeats it.
float() creates a numeric version for the final sentences.
projects.explanation: The original fav_num stays a string, even after a separate numeric variable is created.
projects.note: Both repetition lines print the same result. This is a useful illustration of the difference between conversion and reassignment.

projects.title: Birthday, eggs & cookies
projects.summary: Answer three everyday questions with addition, multiplication, and division.
steps: The entered age becomes the age at the next birthday.
Multiply the number of dozens by twelve.
Divide the cookies by the entered number of people.
projects.explanation: The / operator returns the share per person. A zero divisor is not allowed.
projects.note: The program divides by the entered number of people; it does not add an extra person for the visitor.

projects.title: Dinner, down to the cent
projects.summary: Build a meal bill from prices, guests, drinks, and tax, then calculate change.
steps: Multiply each price by its quantity, then add the results.
Convert a percentage into a fraction and round the tax to two decimals.
Subtract the bill from the cash payment.
projects.explanation: The tax is rounded before the final total and change are calculated.
projects.note: A payment below the total produces negative change in the original. The demo labels it as an amount still owed.

projects.title: How long will it download?
projects.summary: Estimate download time from a file size and a steady transfer speed.
steps: Use megabytes per second to keep units consistent.
Size divided by speed gives seconds.
projects.explanation: Matching the units makes the calculation a single division.
projects.note: This is a constant-speed estimate. The speed must be greater than zero.

projects.title: An arithmetic notebook
projects.summary: Explore type conversions, operator order, remainders, and division.
steps: Convert a string to int, an int to float, and a float to string.
Compare modulo, floor division, and regular division.
Most print statements are commented out, so the file produces no console output.
projects.explanation: Parentheses are evaluated first; multiplication precedes addition and subtraction.
projects.note: The interactive expression explorer is an added teaching aid. Running this original file produces no output.

projects.title: A change in temperature
projects.summary: Convert Fahrenheit into Celsius and format the result to one decimal place.
steps: Subtract 32 and multiply by five ninths.
The .1f format displays one decimal place.
projects.explanation: Parentheses ensure 32 is subtracted before the multiplication.
projects.note: The temperature slider is an added browser control for the same formula.

projects.title: Dinner with a little extra
projects.summary: Extend the meal calculator with a yes-or-no decision and an optional tip.
steps: Reuse the subtotal and rounded sales-tax calculation.
A yes branch reads a tip; a no branch sets it to zero.
Add the tip and calculate change.
projects.explanation: The optional branch is an early example of decisions changing a numeric result.
projects.note: The original expects yes or no. Other answers leave tip_amount undefined. Browser controls offer those two valid choices.

projects.title: Falling with air resistance
projects.summary: Calculate velocity using mass, gravity, time, density, area, and drag.
steps: Calculate c from half the density, area, and drag coefficient.
math.sqrt() and math.exp() describe how velocity approaches a limit.
Print the drag factor and speed to three decimals.
projects.explanation: The exponential term changes with time; the square-root factor sets the limiting velocity.
projects.note: This is the formula used in the assignment, with positive physical inputs and time at least zero. It is a classroom model.

projects.title: A math-module starting point
projects.summary: An unfinished scratch file containing only an import of Python's math module.
steps: import math makes mathematical functions available.
No calculations or print statements have been added in this file.
projects.explanation: Importing a module makes its functions available; it does not print a result by itself.
projects.note: This is a starting point, not a completed calculator. It is included so every Python file is represented.

projects.title: Formatting & formula workshop
projects.summary: Compare string formatting, calculate force, and take a square root.
steps: f-strings and .format() can produce equivalent text.
Multiply mass by acceleration and show four decimals.
Import math and call sqrt() on an entered value.
projects.explanation: Readable variable names make the formula understandable without extra notation.
projects.note: The original uses several formatting demonstrations before asking for inputs. Its full output is preserved in the sample run.

projects.title: Comparisons & a favorite animal
projects.summary: Compare two numbers three ways, then check whether you also like sheep.
steps: Separate if statements test greater-than and equality.
strip().lower() removes surrounding spaces and ignores letter case.
Compare the animal with the stored favorite, sheep.
projects.explanation: Chaining these methods makes a simple text comparison more forgiving.
projects.note: The three number comparisons are independent, so each one prints a result.

projects.title: Rescue Eevee: the first adventure
projects.summary: Pack two supplies, choose a Pokémon, and navigate a branching rescue story.
steps: A loop collects two distinct items from the available supplies.
Each Pokémon opens its own story branches.
Inventory checks determine which actions are available.
projects.explanation: A helper function repeats a prompt until the answer belongs to a list of allowed choices.
projects.note: This first version has no nickname, trust score, berry-feeding ending, or evolution. The browser story keeps that distinction.

projects.title: Did I pass?
projects.summary: Turn a percentage into a letter grade and compare it with a chosen passing mark.
steps: The grade and passing threshold are separate inputs.
An if/elif ladder selects the first matching grade band.
A second ladder applies the exact plus/minus bands in the file.
projects.explanation: The conditions are ordered from highest to lowest so a grade lands in one band.
projects.note: The original prints the final letter twice. It assigns D to 60–66 and does not define a D− band. The browser follows those same bands.

projects.title: Inside & outside an if
projects.summary: Read an annotated introduction to comparisons, indentation, and conditional blocks.
steps: The a == b block does not run because the values differ.
The unindented print runs regardless of that condition.
projects.explanation: Indentation determines what belongs to a branch. The final print is outside the branch.
projects.note: The interactive comparison controls are an added teaching aid. The original uses the fixed values 2 and 3.

projects.title: A classroom loan decision
projects.summary: Explore a fictional decision tree using four ratings from one to ten.
steps: Read loan size, credit history, income, and down payment ratings.
A loan-size rating of five selects the larger-loan branch.
and/or checks decide which other ratings satisfy the classroom rules.
projects.explanation: A nested decision tree makes the next condition depend on the previous result.
projects.note: These are fictional classroom rules, not lending advice or a real eligibility assessment.

projects.title: Rescue Eevee: choices that matter
projects.summary: Return to Whispering Woods with nicknames, trust, special moves, and evolution.
steps: Pack supplies and optionally name a partner.
Choices add trust, consume a berry, or collect a Poké Ball.
Trust of three or more evolves Eevee according to the chosen partner.
projects.explanation: The ending uses accumulated state rather than just the final answer.
projects.note: The illustrated browser adaptation is copied from your existing game. Its written scenes are adapted for the web; the original Python source and sample run are preserved here.

projects.title: Can we ride?
projects.summary: Combine ages, heights, a second rider, and a golden passport into one decision.
steps: Some ages trigger an extra passport question.
A yes answer treats a 12–17-year-old as age 18 for these rules.
Pair and solo requirements use different combinations of age and height.
projects.explanation: Every pair must pass the minimum-height test before any of the age combinations are considered.
projects.note: This models only the assignment's fictional ride rules. The browser result explains which condition matched.

projects.title: Thinking in true & false
projects.summary: Explore Boolean expressions and read class notes on logical operators.
steps: can_graduate is set to None, so the original prints None.
x == 5 or 2 behaves differently from x == 5 or x == 2.
The file also contains a scripture quotation and a combined Boolean example.
projects.explanation: None is a placeholder here, not a completed graduation condition. The code comment asks for a condition to be filled in.
projects.note: The interactive graduation checker completes the condition described in the comments: at least 120 credits and a GPA above 2.0. It is labeled as an added example.

projects.title: Ask again, politely
projects.summary: Keep asking until a number is nonnegative, then keep asking for candy until yes.
steps: while number < 0 repeats the number prompt.
The condition rejects only negatives, even though the prompt says positive.
The candy loop continues until a trimmed, lowercase answer equals yes.
projects.explanation: A while loop checks its condition again after each pass and stops when the condition becomes false.
projects.note: Zero is accepted by the original. The browser uses the same nonnegative-number rule.

projects.title: Six letters. One secret.
projects.summary: Guess a hidden word and use position-by-position clues to find the answer.
steps: A for loop creates one underscore for each secret letter.
A while loop continues until the guess matches. Every attempt is counted, including wrong lengths.
Uppercase means an exact position; lowercase means the letter is elsewhere; an underscore means absent.
projects.explanation: The index lets the program compare the same position in both words before checking membership anywhere in the secret.
projects.note: The original secret is preserved. Unlike Wordle, repeated letters are checked with simple membership and are not limited to the number of occurrences in the secret.

projects.title: Lists and counted loops
projects.summary: Loop through a list of colors and several number patterns to practice repetition.
steps: A for loop takes one item from the list at a time.
range(1, 9) produces the numbers one through eight.
range(2, 21, 2) produces the even numbers through twenty.
projects.explanation: A for loop repeats its body once for each value in an iterable, such as a list or range.
projects.note: This preparation exercise has no input; it prints three small loop demonstrations.

projects.title: Word Quest: choose a category
projects.summary: Guess a hidden word from a chosen category, earn a rank, and unlock a quick bonus round.
steps: Select Book of Mormon, Bible, or general vocabulary words.
A for loop compares each letter and reports exact or misplaced matches.
The while loop limits attempts and a fast win can unlock a bonus guess.
projects.explanation: The loop visits each position in the secret word so the game can compare the guess letter at the same index.
projects.note: This is a terminal game with color, animation, random word selection, and a six-attempt limit. Run the original file locally to play it.

projects.title: Word Quest: the grand adventure
projects.summary: Turn the category game into a full terminal adventure with story branches, scoring, rewards, and a final boss.
steps: A story branch changes the narration before the word round begins.
Games played, wins, score, treasures, and level are stored as state.
Winning can unlock a bonus round, rewards, and eventually a final boss.
projects.explanation: The outer while loop lets the player start another complete round while the game keeps cumulative statistics.
projects.note: This is the expanded terminal version of Word Quest. It includes animated effects and random events, so exact output changes between runs.

projects.title: Count letters in a word
projects.summary: Use for loops to print a word, highlight a favorite letter, and hide a selected letter.
steps: The first loop prints Commitment one character at a time.
Two loops use a favorite letter to uppercase or hide matching characters.
The final loop counts alphabetic characters while formatting every nth letter.
projects.explanation: enumerate() provides both the current position and its value, which is useful when a loop needs an index and an item together.
projects.note: This is a lesson exercise with a stretch challenge; it is preserved as source notes rather than a browser game.

projects.title: A first tour of for loops
projects.summary: Practice range(), string iteration, and looping through a list with small class examples.
steps: range() controls how many times the loop runs.
A for loop can visit each character in a name.
The same loop pattern works with list items.
projects.explanation: range(1, 6) starts at one and stops before six, so the loop prints one through five.
projects.note: These are the original Week 8 class examples, including the input-driven Hello World loop.
